definition: Hesitant means slow to act because of uncertainty.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word hesitant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know hesitant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The new lifeguard was hesitant on his first whistle, unsure whether the swimmers were really too far out.
Unsure is the milder state — you can be unsure and still act quickly; hesitant means the uncertainty is visibly slowing you down.
Paralyzed is far stronger than hesitant: a paralyzed decision-maker cannot act at all, while a hesitant one acts late and haltingly.

Reluctant means unwilling — you drag your feet because you do not want to do the thing at all. Hesitant is about doubt, not desire: a hesitant person usually wants to act and is slowed by uncertainty. A reluctant witness resents being called at all; a hesitant one wants to speak but keeps stalling.

Tentative describes the cautious, unconfident manner of an action, or a plan made only provisionally — a tentative knock, a tentative agreement. Hesitant is about the delay itself: uncertainty slowing you down before you act at all. A tentative step is soft and careful; a hesitant one is late in coming.

The scholarship application sat open on Jun's laptop for eleven days.
He reread the essay prompt each night, typed a sentence, and deleted it.
His teachers had told him he was exactly the kind of candidate the program wanted, but he kept wondering if his grades from freshman year would sink him.
The night before the deadline, the form was still blank.
Jun wasn't lazy or uninterested — he was hesitant, and his uncertainty had nearly cost him the chance.
Jun's slowness to act — eleven days of typing and deleting — flows directly from his uncertainty about his own chances, which is exactly what hesitant means.
Hesitant is the adjective for a person or manner ('a hesitant knock'); its verb cousin hesitate names the pause itself.
Being hesitant is about uncertainty, not refusal — a hesitant person usually wants to act and can't quite start.

The spring musical's auditions ran long, and by four o'clock only two names remained on the sign-up sheet.
Devon wanted the lead badly — he had rehearsed the audition song for weeks and told his friends as much.

Yet when his name was called he stood hesitant in the wings, smoothing the sheet music, stepping toward the stage and back twice, wondering whether his voice had fully recovered from last week's cold.
The director finally waved him forward, and once he began, he sang without a single crack.
Afterward Devon joked that the hardest part of the whole audition had been the six feet between the curtain and the piano.
